title: A dog's sense of smell
hook: A dog's nose is built to smell while it breathes out, not just in.
peek: Dogs have far more smell receptors than people, and their noses are built differently too. A fold inside splits each breath, and side slits let them breathe out without blowing away the scent.
lede: Estimates put a dog's smell receptors at around 300 million, against about 6 million in a person. The design matters as much as the number. When a dog sniffs, a fold of tissue sends part of the air into a separate chamber for smelling. When it breathes out, the air leaves through slits at the sides of the nose, so it does not push the scent away.

bullets.text: A dog on a scent does not take long breaths. It sniffs in short bursts, several times a second, and the air leaving the side slits flows out to the sides and backwards, which helps stir up and draw in fresh scent.
Each nostril takes in air separately, and dogs can compare the two. That helps them work out which direction a smell is coming from, a little like using two ears to place a sound.
Dogs, like many mammals, have a second smelling system above the roof of the mouth. It is thought to pick up chemical signals from other animals that the main nose misses.
In Italy, breeds like the Lagotto Romagnolo are trained to sniff out truffles growing underground in woodland. They have largely replaced pigs, which tend to want the truffle for themselves.
